claim: Helicobacter pylori infects more than half of the world's population.
source: Helicobacter pylori is a helical-shaped, Gram-negative bacteria that infects more than half of the world's population (Hooi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hooi et al., 2017.

claim: Approximately 80% of gastric cancer cases are attributed to H. pylori infection.
source: Chronic infection with H. pylori can cause gastric ulcers and cancers; approximately 80% of gastric cancer cases are attributed to H. pylori infection (de Martel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Martel et al., 2020.

claim: The helical shape of H. pylori cells helps establish colonization of the stomach and promotes immunopathology during infection.
source: The helical shape of H. pylori cells helps establish colonization of the stomach and promotes immunopathology during infection (Martínez et al., 2019; Montecucco and Rappuoli, 2001; Sycuro et al., 2010; Sycuro et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Csd5 is a transmembrane protein that binds directly to PG in the periplasm with its SH3 domain and binds to CcmA in the cytoplasm.
source: Csd5 is a transmembrane protein that binds directly to PG in the periplasm with its SH3 domain and binds to CcmA in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction section describing Csd5 function.

claim: Csd5 interacts with ATP synthase and MurF, independent of interactions with CcmA.
source: Csd5 also interacts with ATP synthase and MurF, an essential PG precursor enzyme that catalyzes the final cytoplasmic PG biosynthesis step, independent of interactions with CcmA (Blair et al., 2018; Hrast et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blair et al., 2018 and Hrast et al., 2013.

claim: Csd7 is a transmembrane protein that stabilizes the PG-hydrolase Csd1.
source: Csd7 is a transmembrane protein that stabilizes the PG-hydrolase Csd1, and Csd2, a catalytically inactive homolog of Csd1.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction section describing Csd7 function.

claim: Weak interactions between Csd7 and CcmA have been detected by co-immunoprecipitation experiments that include cross-linking reagents followed by mass spectrometry.
source: Weak interactions between Csd7 and CcmA have been detected by co-immunoprecipitation experiments that include cross-linking reagents followed by mass spectrometry (Yang et al., 2019), but whether CcmA, Csd7, and Csd5 are all part of one protein complex was unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: CcmA and probes that report on PG synthesis localize to the major helical axis of H. pylori cells.
source: CcmA and probes that report on PG synthesis localize to the major helical axis of H. pylori cells (regions with a Gaussian curvature value of 5 ± 1 µm–2 on a helical cell), indicating that CcmA is in the same region of the cell where increased levels of PG synthesis occur (Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2020.

claim: CcmA is the only bactofilin encoded in the H. pylori genome.
source: CcmA is the only bactofilin encoded in the H. pylori genome.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction section.

claim: Bactofilins are a class of highly conserved, spontaneously polymerizing, cytoskeletal proteins in bacteria.
source: Bactofilins are a class of highly conserved, spontaneously polymerizing, cytoskeletal proteins in bacteria that perform a variety of functions (Bulyha et al., 2013; El Andari et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2017; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Bactofilins modulate cell shape in multiple different bacterial species.
source: Bactofilins are a class of highly conserved, spontaneously polymerizing, cytoskeletal proteins in bacteria that perform a variety of functions (Bulyha et al., 2013; El Andari et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2017; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019) including modulating cell shape in multiple different bacterial species (Brockett et al., 2021; Hay et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2018; Koch et al., 2011; Sycuro et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Bactofilins are identified by the presence of a bactofilin domain (DUF583), which forms a β-helix that is flanked by unstructured terminal regions.
source: Bactofilins are identified by the presence of a bactofilin domain (DUF583), which forms a β-helix that is flanked by unstructured terminal regions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction section describing bactofilin structure.

claim: The N-terminal region of CcmA is composed of amino acids 1–17.
source: The N-terminal region is composed of amino acids 1–17, the bactofilin domain is composed of amino acids 18–118, and the C-terminal region is composed of amino acids 119–136.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment analysis using SWISS-MODEL.

claim: The bactofilin domain of CcmA is composed of amino acids 18–118.
source: The N-terminal region is composed of amino acids 1–17, the bactofilin domain is composed of amino acids 18–118, and the C-terminal region is composed of amino acids 119–136.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment analysis using SWISS-MODEL.

claim: The C-terminal region of CcmA is composed of amino acids 119–136.
source: The N-terminal region is composed of amino acids 1–17, the bactofilin domain is composed of amino acids 18–118, and the C-terminal region is composed of amino acids 119–136.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment analysis using SWISS-MODEL.

claim: The proposed membrane binding motif in CcmA spans amino acids 3–12.
source: It has been proposed that bactofilins contain a short membrane binding motif within their N-terminal regions, which spans amino acids 3–12 in CcmA (Deng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2019.

claim: The bactofilin domain of CcmA forms a right-handed, three-sided, triangular β-helix.
source: RoseTTAFold generated five models of CcmA. In all five, the bactofilin domain forms a three-sided, right-handed β-helix with a left-handed twist (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is based on protein structure prediction using RoseTTAFold and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The N-terminal region of CcmA is unstructured.
source: RoseTTAFold generated five models of CcmA. In all five, the bactofilin domain forms a three-sided, right-handed β-helix with a left-handed twist (Figure 1B), the N-terminal region is unstructured, and part of the C-terminal region forms a short ɑ-helix and caps the end of the bactofilin domain (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on protein structure prediction using RoseTTAFold and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Part of the C-terminal region of CcmA forms a short α-helix and caps the end of the bactofilin domain.
source: RoseTTAFold generated five models of CcmA. In all five, the bactofilin domain forms a three-sided, right-handed β-helix with a left-handed twist (Figure 1B), the N-terminal region is unstructured, and part of the C-terminal region forms a short ɑ-helix and caps the end of the bactofilin domain (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on protein structure prediction using RoseTTAFold and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The N-terminal region and bactofilin domain of CcmA are together necessary and sufficient to pattern the helical shape of H. pylori cells.
source: The N-terminal region and bactofilin domain are together necessary and sufficient to pattern the helical shape of H. pylori cells
evidence: The claim is stated as a section heading and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Cells that lacked either the putative membrane binding motif (∆MM) or the last five amino acids of the N-terminal region (∆13–17) were helical but had slightly different side curvature values than the WT population.
source: Cells that lacked either the putative membrane binding motif (∆MM) or the last five amino acids of the N-terminal region (∆13–17) were helical but had slightly different side curvature values than the WT population, suggesting that the N-terminal region of CcmA may have multiple functional regions within it.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-contrast microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: CD spectra of WT CcmA and the truncation mutants ∆NT, ∆CT, and BD at 20°C all have the characteristic negative peak at 216 nm, indicating β-strand secondary structure.
source: CD spectra of WT CcmA and the truncation mutants ∆NT, ∆CT, and BD at 20°C all look very similar; they have the characteristic negative peak at 216 nm, indicating β-strand secondary structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither terminal region of CcmA is required for the bactofilin domain to fold properly.
source: Together, these data, combined with the modeling by RoseTTAFold in Figure 1C, suggest that CcmA's bactofilin domain very likely forms a β-helix and confirms that neither terminal region is required for the bactofilin domain to fold properly.
evidence: The claim is based on circular dichroism spectroscopy data and RoseTTAFold modeling.

claim: The CD spectra of CcmA point mutants I55A and L110S at 20°C resemble spectra of melted WT CcmA at 95°C.
source: The CD spectra of both mutants (I55A and L110S) at 20°C resemble spectra of melted WT CcmA at 95°C (Figure 3B), suggesting that these proteins are not folded.
evidence: The claim is supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CcmA point mutants I55A and L110S are not folded.
source: The CD spectra of both mutants (I55A and L110S) at 20°C resemble spectra of melted WT CcmA at 95°C (Figure 3B), suggesting that these proteins are not folded.
evidence: The claim is inferred from circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The bactofilin domain alone is capable of polymerization.
source: The bactofilin domain alone is capable of polymerization: the terminal regions of CcmA modulate lateral interactions between CcmA filaments
evidence: The claim is stated as a section heading and supported by TEM data in Figure 4.

claim: WT CcmA polymerizes into small filaments that measure on average 3.04 nm (SD = 0.79, n = 18) in width.
source: As previously reported (Holtrup et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2020), WT CcmA polymerizes into small filaments that measure on average 3.04 nm (SD = 0.79, n = 18) in width.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data and citations to previous work.

claim: WT CcmA filaments wrap together to form bundles of approximately 21.34 nm (SD = 4.82, n = 24) wide.
source: The filaments wrap together to form bundles of approximately 21.34 nm (SD = 4.82, n = 24) wide, and form lattice structures (Figure 4A and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4A and G.

claim: WT CcmA forms lattice structures.
source: The filaments wrap together to form bundles of approximately 21.34 nm (SD = 4.82, n = 24) wide, and form lattice structures (Figure 4A and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4A and G.

claim: ∆NT CcmA formed filaments and bundles that were more homogenous, straighter, and thinner than WT and failed to form lattice structures.
source: ∆NT formed filaments and bundles that were more homogenous, straighter, and thinner than WT and appear to only contain 2–4 filaments each. ∆NT failed to form lattice structures (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ∆MM CcmA resembled WT CcmA, forming filaments and bundles of approximately the same width as WT and formed lattices.
source: ∆MM resembled WT CcmA, forming filaments and bundles of approximately the same width as WT and formed lattices (Figure 4C and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4C and G.

claim: ∆13–17 CcmA resembled ∆NT CcmA.
source: ∆13–17 resembled ∆NT (Figure 4D and G), suggesting that amino acids 13–17 are responsible for filament bundling properties of ∆NT.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4D and G.

claim: Amino acids 13–17 of CcmA are responsible for filament bundling properties.
source: ∆13–17 resembled ∆NT (Figure 4D and G), suggesting that amino acids 13–17 are responsible for filament bundling properties of ∆NT.
evidence: The claim is inferred from TEM data comparing ∆13–17 and ∆NT mutants.

claim: ∆CT CcmA formed bundles that were wider than WT CcmA but failed to form lattices.
source: ∆CT formed bundles that were wider than WT CcmA but failed to form lattices (Figure 4E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4E and G.

claim: BD CcmA formed straight bundles that were narrower than those found in WT samples and failed to form lattices.
source: Lastly, BD formed straight bundles that were narrower than those found in WT samples and failed to form lattices (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The bactofilin domain is sufficient for polymerization of CcmA.
source: These data suggest that the bactofilin domain is sufficient for polymerization of CcmA while the N- and C-terminal regions of CcmA regulate interpolymer interactions that impact the width of bundles by modulating the number of filaments that form a bundle, and the ability of CcmA to form lattices.
evidence: The claim is inferred from TEM data showing that BD mutant can polymerize.

claim: The N- and C-terminal regions of CcmA regulate interpolymer interactions that impact the width of bundles by modulating the number of filaments that form a bundle.
source: These data suggest that the bactofilin domain is sufficient for polymerization of CcmA while the N- and C-terminal regions of CcmA regulate interpolymer interactions that impact the width of bundles by modulating the number of filaments that form a bundle, and the ability of CcmA to form lattices.
evidence: The claim is inferred from TEM data comparing different CcmA truncation mutants.

claim: The ability of CcmA to polymerize is not sufficient to pattern the helical shape of H. pylori cells.
source: Taken together with our experiments from Figure 2, where we expressed the truncated versions of CcmA in H. pylori, these data suggest that the ability of CcmA to polymerize is not sufficient to pattern the helical shape of H. pylori cells and in vitro lattice formation does not correlate with helical cell shape.
evidence: The claim is inferred from combining cell shape data (Figure 2) and polymerization data (Figure 4).

claim: In vitro lattice formation does not correlate with helical cell shape.
source: Taken together with our experiments from Figure 2, where we expressed the truncated versions of CcmA in H. pylori, these data suggest that the ability of CcmA to polymerize is not sufficient to pattern the helical shape of H. pylori cells and in vitro lattice formation does not correlate with helical cell shape.
evidence: The claim is inferred from combining cell shape data (Figure 2) and polymerization data (Figure 4).

claim: CcmA's bactofilin domain mediates interactions with Csd5 and Csd7.
source: CcmA's bactofilin domain mediates interactions with Csd5 and Csd7, and the N-terminal region of CcmA inhibits interactions with Csd7
evidence: The claim is stated as a section heading and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5.

claim: All mutant versions of CcmA except ∆CT were detected by Western blotting in Csd5-FLAG IP fractions.
source: When we immunoprecipitated Csd5-FLAG, all mutant versions of CcmA were detected by Western blotting of the IP fractions, except for the ∆CT mutant (Figure 5A), though it is likely that this mutant can still interact with Csd5-FLAG.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The ∆CT mutant of CcmA can interact with Csd5.
source: We found that both ∆CT-HaloTag and BD-HaloTag were expressed at comparable levels as CcmA-HaloTag and could be pulled down by Csd5-FLAG. These three pieces of evidence lead us to conclude that the ∆CT mutant can interact with Csd5, suggesting that only the bactofilin domain is required for interactions between CcmA and Csd5-FLAG.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only the bactofilin domain is required for interactions between CcmA and Csd5.
source: These three pieces of evidence lead us to conclude that the ∆CT mutant can interact with Csd5, suggesting that only the bactofilin domain is required for interactions between CcmA and Csd5-FLAG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data showing that BD mutant interacts with Csd5.

claim: WT CcmA was not able to be detected in Csd7-FLAG IP fractions by Western blotting above background levels.
source: When we immunoprecipitated Csd7-FLAG, we found that, as previously reported (Yang et al., 2019), WT CcmA was not able to be detected in the IP fractions by Western blotting above background levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Versions of CcmA lacking the N-terminal region were robustly co-purified by Csd7.
source: However, versions of CcmA lacking the N-terminal region were robustly co-purified by Csd7 (Figure 5B), suggesting that the N-terminal region inhibits WT CcmA from being co-immunoprecipitated by Csd7-FLAG.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The N-terminal region of CcmA inhibits WT CcmA from being co-immunoprecipitated by Csd7-FLAG.
source: However, versions of CcmA lacking the N-terminal region were robustly co-purified by Csd7 (Figure 5B), suggesting that the N-terminal region inhibits WT CcmA from being co-immunoprecipitated by Csd7-FLAG.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data comparing WT and ∆NT CcmA interactions with Csd7.

claim: Csd5 never co-purified with Csd7 in any of the conditions tested.
source: We found that in all the conditions we tested Csd5 never co-purified with Csd7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CcmA forms separate complexes with Csd5 and Csd7.
source: Together, these data suggest that the bactofilin domain of CcmA mediates interaction with Csd5 and Csd7, the N-terminal region of CcmA inhibits interaction with Csd7, and CcmA forms separate complexes with Csd5 and Csd7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data showing that Csd5 and Csd7 do not co-purify.

claim: Versions of CcmA lacking the C-terminal region are expressed at comparable levels to WT CcmA.
source: Our data also show that versions of CcmA lacking the C-terminal region are expressed at comparable levels to WT CcmA, although they are not recognized as robustly by the ɑ-CcmA polyclonal antibody.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the strain lacking the N-terminal region (∆NT) Csd1 levels are lower than in a strain expressing WT CcmA.
source: As predicted, we found that in the strain lacking the N-terminal region (∆NT) Csd1 levels are lower than in a strain expressing WT CcmA (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: In H. pylori strains lacking the N-terminal region of CcmA, Csd7-Csd1 interactions are decreased in comparison to when WT CcmA is expressed.
source: We found that in H. pylori strains lacking the N-terminal region of CcmA, Csd7-Csd1 interactions are decreased in comparison to when WT CcmA is expressed (Figure 6C), suggesting that when the N-terminal region of CcmA is deleted CcmA-Csd7 interactions increase and inhibit Csd7 from stabilizing Csd1, causing decreased Csd1 levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When the N-terminal region of CcmA is deleted CcmA-Csd7 interactions increase and inhibit Csd7 from stabilizing Csd1, causing decreased Csd1 levels.
source: We found that in H. pylori strains lacking the N-terminal region of CcmA, Csd7-Csd1 interactions are decreased in comparison to when WT CcmA is expressed (Figure 6C), suggesting that when the N-terminal region of CcmA is deleted CcmA-Csd7 interactions increase and inhibit Csd7 from stabilizing Csd1, causing decreased Csd1 levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot data.

claim: Csd1 stability is indirectly regulated by CcmA via Csd7.
source: Our data suggests that Csd1 stability is indirectly regulated by CcmA via Csd7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that CcmA-Csd7 interactions affect Csd1 levels.

claim: Cells that expressed CcmA-HaloTag as the sole copy of CcmA were still helical but had slightly lower-side curvature than WT cells.
source: We found that cells that expressed CcmA-HaloTag as the sole copy of CcmA were still helical but had slightly lower-side curvature than WT cells; adding a second copy of ccmA at rdxA generated cells with side curvature more similar to WT cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell shape analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Adding a second copy of ccmA at rdxA generated cells with side curvature more similar to WT cells.
source: We found that cells that expressed CcmA-HaloTag as the sole copy of CcmA were still helical but had slightly lower-side curvature than WT cells; adding a second copy of ccmA at rdxA generated cells with side curvature more similar to WT cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell shape analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: In WT cells, CcmA-HaloTag signal is present as foci and small arcs that colocalize with the cell envelope.
source: In WT cells, we found that CcmA-HaloTag signal is present as foci and small arcs that colocalize with the cell envelope (white signal) and there were some foci in the center of the cell (Figure 7A, top row).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In cells lacking csd5, there appears to be more CcmA-HaloTag signal in the center of cells than associated with the cell envelope.
source: In cells lacking csd5, there appears to be more CcmA-HaloTag signal in the center of cells than associated with the cell envelope (Figure 7A, fourth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In cells lacking csd7, cells are slightly curved and CcmA-HaloTag signal colocalizes with the cell envelope.
source: In cells lacking csd7, cells are slightly curved and CcmA-HaloTag signal colocalizes with the cell envelope; however, there are also some foci in the center of the cell (Figure 7A, third row).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Loss of Csd5 causes substantially less CcmA to localize to the cell envelope.
source: Loss of Csd5 causes substantially less CcmA to localize to the cell envelope, instead CcmA accumulates in the center of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D SIM microscopy data and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Csd5 recruits CcmA to the cell envelope.
source: These data suggest that Csd5 recruits CcmA to the cell envelope.
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy data showing that CcmA localization depends on Csd5.

claim: If helical cell shape is disrupted while Csd5 is still present, Csd5 directs CcmA to regions of negative Gaussian curvature.
source: If helical cell shape is disrupted (due to loss of another cell shape protein) while Csd5 is still present, Csd5 directs CcmA to regions of negative Gaussian curvature.
evidence: The claim is inferred from curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Csd5, not Csd7, controls CcmA localization.
source: Additionally, the finding that CcmA localization phenotypes are the same in a ∆csd5 mutant and a ∆csd5/7 double mutant suggest that Csd5, not Csd7, controls CcmA localization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing CcmA localization in ∆csd5 and ∆csd5/7 mutants.

claim: In WT cells, CcmA-HaloTag is enriched at the major helical axis (Gaussian curvature value of 5 ± 1 µm–2).
source: In WT cells, CcmA-HaloTag is enriched at the major helical axis (Gaussian curvature value of 5 ± 1 µm–2; Taylor et al., 2020); enrichment peaks at +3.35 µm–2 to +5.31 µm–2 Gaussian curvature and is depleted at Gaussian curvature values lower than +0.97 µm–2 and higher than +6.67 µm–2.
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data and a citation to Taylor et al., 2020.

claim: In all cell-shape-mutant strains, CcmA-HaloTag is depleted at regions of Gaussian curvature where CcmA-HaloTag is enriched in WT cells (+3.35 µm–2 to +5.31 µm–2).
source: In contrast, in all other strains, CcmA-HaloTag is depleted at regions of Gaussian curvature where CcmA-HaloTag is enriched in WT cells (+3.35 µm–2 to +5.31 µm–2), although those Gaussian curvature values are still present in all cell-shape-mutant populations (Figure 7C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: In ∆csd6 mutants, CcmA-HaloTag is enriched at negative Gaussian curvature values.
source: In ∆csd6 and ∆csd7 mutants, CcmA-HaloTag is enriched at negative Gaussian curvature values. In ∆csd6 mutants, enrichment peaks at and continues to be enriched at all values lower than +0.11 µm–2 Gaussian curvature (to –4 µm–2 Gaussian curvature).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In ∆csd7 mutants, CcmA-HaloTag enrichment peaks at +0.15 µm–2 and is enriched at all values below +0.15 µm–2 (to –5.4 µm–2 Gaussian curvature).
source: In ∆csd7 mutants, CcmA-HaloTag enrichment peaks at +0.15 µm–2 and is enriched at all values below +0.15 µm–2 (to –5.4 µm–2 Gaussian curvature; Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In ∆csd5 mutants, CcmA-HaloTag is depleted at negative Gaussian curvature values.
source: In contrast to ∆csd6 and ∆csd7 mutants, in ∆csd5 mutants, CcmA-HaloTag is depleted at negative Gaussian curvature values (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In a ∆csd5/7 double mutant, the CcmA-HaloTag enrichment pattern mirrors the ∆csd5 mutant enrichment pattern.
source: Interestingly, in a ∆csd5/7 double mutant, the CcmA-HaloTag enrichment pattern mirrors the ∆csd5 mutant enrichment pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Csd5 is required for CcmA to localize to the cell envelope.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Csd5 directs CcmA to the cell envelope; CcmA is unable to localize to the cell envelope without Csd5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy and curvature enrichment analysis data.

claim: CcmA is unable to localize to the cell envelope without Csd5.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Csd5 directs CcmA to the cell envelope; CcmA is unable to localize to the cell envelope without Csd5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy and curvature enrichment analysis data.

claim: Csd5 is the primary driver of CcmA localization in WT cells.
source: The finding that in a ∆csd5/∆csd7 double mutant the CcmA-HaloTag localization resembles a ∆csd5 mutant indicates that Csd5, not Csd7, is the primary driver of CcmA localization in WT cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing CcmA localization in ∆csd5 and ∆csd5/7 mutants.

claim: The ∆csd5ccmA∆NT strain has a curved rod phenotype and low levels of Csd1.
source: As shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, the ∆csd5ccmA∆NT strain has a curved rod phenotype and low levels of Csd1 supporting the second possibility, further reinforcing our hypothesis that Csd5 and Csd7 are part of separate protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell shape and Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Csd5 and Csd7 are part of separate protein complexes.
source: As shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, the ∆csd5ccmA∆NT strain has a curved rod phenotype and low levels of Csd1 supporting the second possibility, further reinforcing our hypothesis that Csd5 and Csd7 are part of separate protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that CcmA ∆NT can interact with Csd7 even without Csd5.

claim: CcmA participates in two separate helical-cell-shape-generating protein complexes.
source: We clarify that CcmA participates in two separate helical-cell-shape-generating protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and localization data.

claim: Bactofilins can influence PG sacculus structure by modulating the protein stability of a PG hydrolase.
source: Additionally, these studies reveal that bactofilins can influence PG sacculus structure by modulating the protein stability of a PG hydrolase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that CcmA affects Csd1 stability via Csd7.

claim: In one protein complex, CcmA's bactofilin domain interacts with the cytoplasmic N-terminal region of the transmembrane protein Csd5 directing CcmA to the cell envelope.
source: In one protein complex, CcmA's bactofilin domain interacts with the cytoplasmic N-terminal region of the transmembrane protein Csd5 directing CcmA to the cell envelope.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and localization data.

claim: Csd5 brings MurF and PG precursors to the same region of the cell envelope for new PG to be inserted into the cell wall.
source: Csd5 brings MurF and PG precursors to the same region of the cell envelope for new PG to be inserted into the cell wall.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: CcmA's N-terminal region inhibits interaction of CcmA's bactofilin domain, which allows Csd7 to stabilize Csd1.
source: CcmA's N-terminal region inhibits interaction of CcmA's bactofilin domain, which allows Csd7 to stabilize Csd1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot data and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: When the N-terminus of CcmA is removed, interactions between Csd7 and CcmA are stabilized and Csd1 is no longer detected in the Csd7 complex.
source: When the N-terminus of CcmA is removed, interactions between Csd7 and CcmA are stabilized and Csd1 is no longer detected in the Csd7 complex (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: Csd7 cannot simultaneously interact with Csd1 and CcmA.
source: Steady-state levels of Csd1 are depleted in the ccmA ΔNT mutant, suggesting that Csd7 cannot simultaneously interact with Csd1 and CcmA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot data.

claim: Loss of the N-terminus of CcmA results in lower levels of Csd1, generating curved-rod-shaped cells.
